listings.name: Ultra Music Festival
listings.content: Streets of downtown Miami. People from around the world flock to Miami every March for its notorious Ultra Music Festival. It’s a three-day and -night festival that includes the most famous DJs in the music industry. Tickets usually range from $300–600 from the three-day festival and increase in price as it gets closer to the show in March. The show sells out almost every year so be sure to get your tickets as soon as possible.

listings.name: Calle Ocho
listings.content: The largest Hispanic street festival in Miami. It’s a one-day festival that features contests, concerts and food. There is also a carnival that takes place in a lot to the left of Florida International University’s main entrance. The carnival is on the same day as Calle Ocho. The festival is usually held in March on Calle Ocho. It is free except for parking if you bring your car.

listings.name: Carnaval Miami
listings.content: A festival that consists of ten events along the course of ten days during the weeks of late February and early March. The Kiwanis club of little Havana (little Cuba) hosts this festival full of music, international foods, concerts, sports, culinary competitions, galas and upscale Latin jazz festival.

listings.name: Independence Day
listings.content: City-wide. Held on July 4. The Miami skyline is illuminated by fireworks on the “birth date” of the United States. While Key Biscayne has great views of the fireworks show, Bayfront Park has live music as well as a laser show.

listings.name: King Mango Strut
listings.content: Held after Christmas, this parade began as a parody of current events as well as the Orange Bowl Parade. The Orange Bowl Parade, unlike its famous Rose Bowl counterpart, is no longer held anymore, but the King Mango Strut is still having a good time making fun of the previous year’s follies.
listings.address: Main Avenue and Grand Avenue in Coconut Grove

listings.name: Barnacle Historic State Park
listings.content: One of the oldest homes in Dade County, built in 1891 on the shore of Biscayne Bay. Offers a glimpse of Old Florida during The Era of the Bay. Situated on the shore of Biscayne Bay, this was the home of Ralph Middleton Munroe, one of Coconut Grove´s most charming and influential pioneers. Today, the estate is one of the last remnants of the once vast Miami Hammock, the term for the wooded area that grew around the Miami river valley. Two buildings remain, the main house and the boathouse, with attached boat launch. Enjoy sitting in the rocking chairs on the spacious porch used as a gathering place or on a bench under a tree for solitude. The forest surrounding the home is hardwood hammock and is the last of its kind in the area. The unique architecture includes period furniture and wide porches that afford magnificent views.
listings.price: $2 to enter the park, collected by honor system in a drop box; under age 6 enter free. More for a tour of the building

listings.name: Vizcaya Museum and Gardens
listings.content: Pseudo-Italian estate built by James Deering, of the International Harvester fortune. Includes a main house filled with art and furnishings and ten acres of gardens on Biscayne Bay. $25 adults, $10 children 6-12. Admission is free for children 5 years of age or younger. Must purchase tickets online. While this is described as something of an art museum, this is much more one of those museums that just preserved a really rich guy's house the way it was when he died, including the art with the occasional traveling exhibit.

listings.name: Plymouth Congregational Church
listings.content: Completed in 1917, this church was built by a single man using only a hatchet, a trowel, a plumb line, and a T-square. Its architectural style was modeled after the old Spanish missions of Mexico.

listings.name: Coconut Grove Playhouse
listings.content: A South Florida landmark that hosted live theater from 1956-2006. It is closed and awaiting restoration.

listings.name: The Kampong
listings.content: An 8-acre (32,000 m²) tropical garden that forms part of the National Tropical Botanical Garden.

listings.name: Casa Xabi
listings.content: Delicious but extremely pricey Basque restaurant.

listings.name: Barracuda Bar and Grill
listings.content: This throw back to the old Grove is a "come as you are" locals spot. Enjoy their nice beer selection and shoot a game of pool or play some darts. Not expensive and open late it's always a fun time.

listings.name: Sandbar Grill
listings.content: There are 20 televisions in this bar. The menu has seafood specialties and $0.25 wings on Mondays. Sandbar also has theme nights like the "White Trash Bash."

listings.name: Greenstreet Cafe
listings.content: – Serves breakfast, lunch, and dinner. A bit more upscale but has a fantastic outside seating area for cocktails.

listings.name: Vinoteca
listings.content: A quiet wine bar with a wildly extensive selection.

listings.name: Mayfair Hotel & Spa
listings.content: Blending New York influences with the tropical vibe of Miami, the iconic Mayfair Hotel & Spa - poised in hip Coconut Grove - unveils a new layer of haute with the opening of rooftop Cabana One Lounge & Pool Club and famed New York steakhouse Angelo & Maxie’s. Gaudi-inspired design and an unpretentious ambience define this historic enclave, complete with an orchid-filled, open-air atrium, Japanese soaking tubs on private bougainvillea-covered terraces and a fully sustainable Jurlique Spa.

listings.name: The Mutiny Hotel
listings.content: The hotel's 12-story tower sits on Sailboat Bay. The hotel's 120 one- and two-bedroom suites all have bay or city views. While this hotel's past as a bastion of the Miami criminal underworld and artistic demimonde is the stuff of legend, the vibe now is much more old white people and an empty Mexican restaurant.

listings.name: The Ritz-Carlton
listings.content: This luxury hotel has a charming, Italian villa-like ambience that takes its cue from nearby historic mansion, Villa Vizcaya. With abundant roses, soaring ceilings, commanding Venetian stucco columns, a grand fireplace, sleek marble floor and soaring glass wall with views onto a garden courtyard and waterfall fountain, it is a relaxing respite within one of Miami’s most noteworthy neighborhoods. Savor Italian cuisine in Bizcaya lounge, renowned for its Tuscan-influenced fare and the area’s only upscale live music venue every Thursday through Saturday, or be pampered in the city’s finest Boutique Spa. Beautifully renovated Miami boutique hotel rooms offer views of the lush neighborhood or Biscayne Bay and are close to shopping, attractions, and Miami’s downtown financial district.

listings.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami
listings.content: This one is good if you like trying to figure out if it's you or the painting that is touched.

listings.name: Haitian Heritage Museum
listings.content: Founded in 2004 to commemorate Haiti’s bicentennial independence.

listings.name: Design District Gallery Walk
listings.content: Taking place during the second Saturday of each month, this is an evening of art, dining, cocktails and other events in the Design District.

listings.name: MC Kitchen
listings.content: Modern Italian cuisine by Chef Dena Marino.

listings.name: Kush
listings.content: Gastropub with a good local beer selection.

listings.name: Bayfront Park
listings.content: This park has two amphitheaters (one large and a one smaller) and hosts live performances. This park also has memorials for the astronauts who perished in the Challenger spaceship accident, former president John F. Kennedy (the JFK Torch of Friendship), and a fountain dedicated to Claude Pepper, a distinguished US congressman.

listings.name: Miami Circle
listings.content: An archaeological site — a 38 circle of holes and wood claimed to date back somewhere between 1,700 and 2,000 years old.

listings.name: Brickell Key
listings.content: An island community, attached to Brickell by a pedestrian friendly bridge. It is home to the famed Mandarin Oriental hotel. Strollers along Brickell Key often spot one of the many giant iguanas that make the island their home.

listings.name: Jungle Island
listings.content: Formerly Parrot Jungle, it's a lush tropical garden that features animal shows and exhibits. Animal encounters are available for an additional charge.

listings.name: Miami Seaquarium
listings.content: This 38-acre tropical island paradise features marine shows and marine life exhibits. Expect to stay around 2-3 hours touring the large aquarium. 10 minutes from downtown Miami and directly adjacent to Fairchild Tropical Botanical Garden.

listings.name: Miami Children's Museum
listings.content: Parking available for $2/hr.

listings.name: Gesu Church
listings.content: Historic Roman Catholic church, built in 1896.

listings.name: Trinity Episcopal Cathedral
listings.content: Built in 1925, this is the cathedral church of the Episcopal Diocese of Southeast Florida.

listings.name: Bayside Marketplace
listings.content: Shopping, dining, and special boat tours of surrounding islands, including the island where celebrities live.

listings.name: Kaseya Center
listings.content: In addition to Miami Heat (an NBA team) games being played here, this arena has hosted several awards shows in its past such as the MTV Video Music Awards (twice). Several concerts are also held here. Call box office for ticket information.

listings.name: Simpson Park Hammock
listings.content: Urban park and nature preserve

listings.name: Alice Wainwright Park
listings.content: Waterfront park and nature preserve.

listings.name: Club Space Miami
listings.content: Voted best U.S. club at the IDMA 2011 Awards. Known for its Saturday nights. There are multiple rooms with different genres of music in each room so you can choose from a wide variety. They hold events almost every weekend with themed parties and well known/famous DJs.

listings.name: Novecento
listings.content: A very popular Argentinian-style restaurant and bar. There is a variety of casual and fine dining options.

listings.name: Cajun Boil Brickell
listings.content: Seafood dishes.

listings.name: Blackbird Ordinary
listings.content: Cocktails and culturally inspired food.

listings.name: Rosa Sky
listings.content: A lively rooftop lounge.

listings.name: Hilton Miami Downtown
listings.content: 527-room hotel.

listings.name: InterContinental Miami
listings.content: 5-star hotel. 641 rooms and 34 suites, offering views of the skyline and Biscayne Bay. 66,000 square feet of meeting space, including 30 meeting and conference rooms.

listings.name: Miami Marriott Biscayne Bay
listings.content: All of the rooms offer some sort of view of the bay with a balcony.

listings.name: Hilton Garden Inn Miami Brickell South
listings.content: An urban boutique hotel that features stylish accommodations and exceptional services.

listings.name: Holiday Inn Port of Miami Downtown
Hotel AKA Brickell (formerly The Conrad)
listings.content: It sounded better as The Conrad, but alas, things change.

listings.name: Four Seasons Hotel Miami
listings.content: Has a large pool deck at the seventh-floor lobby level with a view of Biscayne Bay. This hotel takes more on an arty approach to impress you, having some rare paintings and the decor to go with it. Expect everything you will from any other Four Seasons. In your expectations include that the staff will have the "Miami-tude".

listings.name: Mandarin Oriental Hotel
listings.content: From the Mandarin Hotel Group. This is considered the most luxurious (and expensive) of them all. The facilities are top notch and so are the staff (depending on when you go, their turnover is way higher than it should be for a luxury chain of this size and reputation). It is commonplace to find rappers and A-listers in the pool or walking through the lobby. It is also isolated on its own island (Brickell Key) which to some seems more of a hassle than an amenity.

listings.name: Tower Theater
listings.content: A prominent Art Deco landmark on Calle Ocho, airing movies subtitled in Spanish.

listings.name: Gomez Park
listings.content: A small park at the intersection of Calle Ocho and SW 15th Ave, named in honor of Maximo Gomez, the commander of the Cuban troops during its War of Independence in the late 19th century. 15th Ave between Calle Ocho and 9th St is paved with a beautiful wavy brick pattern with images of dominoes, and there are domino motifs throughout the design of the park, which owe its influence to the large crowd of 55-year-old-and-up men who gather here every day to play this and other tabletop games. In case you're wondering: yes, they do card. Visitors, of course, are welcome to observe the greatest center of public street life in Little Havana.

listings.name: Cuban Memorial Boulevard
listings.content: The median along this boulevard is home to many statues and monuments, including an eternal flame burning in memory of the Bay of Pigs Invasion in 1961, a statue commemorating Bay of Pigs brigade member Nestor 'Tony' Izquierdo, a large relief map of Cuba with a quote by Cuban independence leader José Martí, and many others. If you look carefully at the massive ceiba tree located here, with its large, above-ground roots, you might see piles or bags of chicken bones, which are ritual sacrifices by practitioners of the Afro-Cuban religion of Santeria.

listings.name: loanDepot Park
listings.content: One of the newer stadiums in Major League Baseball, loanDepot Park opened in April 2012 as Marlins Park at the former site of the Orange Bowl as the new home of the renamed Miami Marlins. The futuristic, retractable-roof park broke new ground in ballpark architecture; at the insistence of the team's then-owner Jeffrey Loria, it is designed to reflect the culture of 21st-century Miami. Check website or call the toll-free number for tickets to Marlins games.

listings.name: Little Havana Food Tour
listings.content: in Little Havana, a lively, family-friendly neighborhood, and begin a guided edible journey through one of Miami’s oldest neighborhoods. Learn about traditional, rustic Cuban cuisine by tasting your way through the must-visit street in the area — Calle Ocho.

listings.name: Versailles Restaurant and Bakery
listings.content: A prominent gathering place and political forum for the Cuban-American community. The desserts here are delicious.

listings.name: Azucar Ice Cream Company, LLC
listings.content: This "only in Miami" scoop shop, creates artisanal gourmet ice creams and tropical fruit sorbets in Cuban and Latin American inspired flavors. Flavors include Guava, Mamey, Mango and Key Lime Pie ice creams. Signature Miami flavors such as Abuela Maria (vanilla, guava, cream cheese and Maria cookies) and Cuban Rum Cake (vanilla, rum cake and walnuts) are local favs.

listings.name: Yambo Restaurant
listings.content: Nicaraguan. Has a take-away area and a sit-down restaurant decorated in Nicaraguan style.

listings.name: La Carreta
listings.content: Cuban. The flagship restaurant of a small chain of Cuban restaurants (including one location at Miami International Airport). The majority of staff speak limited English but menus are available in English and Spanish. $5–22 per person, per meal.

listings.name: Sanguich
listings.content: An excellent Cuban sandwich shop that also has good coffee and milkshakes.

listings.name: Los Pinareños Fruteria
listings.content: An authentic Latin American open-air fruit market that sells fruit smoothies and coffee, but they are best known for their sugar cane juice.

listings.name: Cubaocho
listings.content: Extensive rum collection and art work.

listings.name: Jefferson House
listings.content: Built in the 1920s it is one of few "grand hotels" in Little Havana.

listings.name: Lagniappe
listings.content: Restaurant and wine bar with live music.

listings.name: Sabor a Peru
listings.content: This place may appear to be a small hole in the wall restaurant but it is extremely well maintained and upkept and usually has a short wait for a table. They also offer take out and delivery. This venue is very popular. If you haven't tried Peruvian food before you must order the Ceviche (Fish/Seafood) and the Lomo Saltado (Beef).

listings.name: Hampton Inn & Suites — Miami Wynwood Design District
Coppertone Sign
listings.content: The original "Coppertone Sign" which has been preserved by the City of Miami. One of MiMo Boulevard's most famous landmarks.

listings.name: New Yorker Boutique Hotel
listings.content: An upscale boutique hotel, built inside the shell of a 1953 motel designed by Norman Giller (a famous post World War II modern architect).

listings.name: Selina Miami Gold Dust
listings.content: Hostel with outdoor pool and restaurant in retrofitted motor lodge building.

listings.name: Vagabond Hotel
listings.content: Newly renovated with 45 loft-like, spacious rooms, an Olympic style pool, Cabana bar and Googie's Diner.

listings.name: Lyric Theater
listings.content: Built by Geder Walker, this theater was opened in 1913 and was a major African-American entertainment destination until the 1960s. Performers from Count Basie to BB King to Aretha Franklin have performed there. Do not enter, this place is gated off and it does not function as a theater any longer.

listings.name: D.A. Dorsey House
listings.content: Home of the first African-American millionaire in Miami. It is a private home, so don't expect to get a tour of the place.

listings.name: Old Black Police Precinct
listings.content: Used from 1950 to 1962, when the Precinct was finally integrated with the main police station.

places.title: 1973 Miami Beach firebombing
places.blurb: On February 2, 1973, a man walked into the crowded Concord Cafeteria in Miami Beach, Florida, poured gasoline out of a large jar, lit a match, ignited the gasoline, and ran out of the cafeteria.
